extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants / principal investigators (especially biomedical researchers) deciding whether to revise/resubmit a triaged application
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for PIs on whether to revise and resubmit (A1/A0) NIH grant applications that were triaged/unscored on the initial submission, weighing empirical success rates, review content, timing, and strategic options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed funding rates for triaged A0 applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical percent funded for unscored (triaged) A0s: overall at NIH 2.3% of new R01s that were 'not scored' as A0s were funded as A1s (range 0.0%–8.4% across ICs); 8.7% of renewals (Type 2) unscored as A0s were funded as A1s (range 0.0%–25.7%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these low baseline probabilities when estimating expected value of resubmission; note the dataset excluded ARRA funds and solicited applications and did not include some FY2013 funding, so actual rates might be slightly higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown resubmission denominator (who actually resubmitted?)
rubrics_metrics.description: The published spreadsheet does not indicate how many initially-triaged A0 applications were actually resubmitted as A1s, which affects the interpretation of funding percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before concluding resubmission is futile, account for the proportion of triaged A0s that were resubmitted. Example: NIDA listed 394 unscored Type 1 apps of which 11 (2.8%) were eventually funded—if only half were resubmitted the effective success rate among resubmitted apps would be ~5.6%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application type matters (Type 1 new vs Type 2 renewal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewals/competing continuations (Type 2) tend to have higher odds of being funded after an initial triage than new (Type 1) applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check IC-specific differences (examples: NIDA 2.8% for Type1 vs 15.2% for Type2; NIAAA 4.7% vs 9.8%). Factor application type into resubmission decisions—renewals may be worth resubmitting more often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of reviewer comments: actionable vs fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviews read like 'revise and resubmit' (specific, fixable issues) versus 'don't waste your time' (non-actionable or fatal critiques) should guide whether to resubmit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the pink sheets carefully: if reviewers give clear options for revision (clarifying a missed point, adding prelim data that you can obtain, etc.), resubmission may be worthwhile; if critiques are non-specific or indicate fundamental flaws, scrapping/rethinking may be better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of triage (consistent poor scores vs split reviews)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triage due to uniform poor scoring across reviewers is harder to overcome than a triage caused by a single reviewer trashing an otherwise positive set of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the triage reflects a split (some reviewers enthusiastic, one very negative), the flaw may be fixable (writing/communication); if the triage reflects broad consensus of poor quality, revision is unlikely to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which criterion scores are weak (Approach vs Significance/Innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific scored criteria that were low matter: poor Approach with good Significance/Innovation is often fixable; poor Significance or Innovation is far harder to remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize resubmission when weaknesses are methodological/approach-oriented and can be addressed; if Significance/Innovation were generally poor, consider major restructuring or abandoning the project for resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior submission / review history of the idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Many A0 submissions are reworkings of previously reviewed ideas; applications with prior favorable review history or prior iterations may have a higher chance of eventual funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether your A0 is effectively a new submission of an idea that already had review exposure—if so, that prior vetting can improve odds (due to improved craft, new prelim data, or gradual convincing of study section/Program).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and submission-cycle constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: NIH deadlines: new applications are submitted one month and amended (A1) applications are due the next month; this affects whether you can submit a new A0 immediately or must wait for the next round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you're close to an A1 deadline and under grant pressure, resubmitting the A1 may be the only option. Conversely, if you can wait and substantially revise, delaying for a new A0 (if strategic) may be preferable—factor calendar timing into decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity cost and PI time/resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Resubmission is time-consuming (one commenter estimated ~50 hours to substantially revise an R01) and takes time away from manuscripts, new research, family, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the expected marginal benefit of resubmitting against alternative uses of your time and resources. If expected funding probability × value is low, the time may be better spent elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic choice: resubmit as A1 vs submit a new A0 or change mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Options include revising and resubmitting as an A1, submitting a 'new' A0 (which risks being re-designated as A1 if too similar), changing mechanism (e.g., R21 → R01 or vice versa), or peeling off an Aim into a different application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resubmitting as an A0 to avoid a 'black mark' only works if the new A0 is meaningfully different; NIH may reject or reassign A0s that are essentially A1s. Consider creating distinct aims, adding new data, or changing mechanism to legitimately count as a new application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer continuity and study section culture
rubrics_metrics.description: The same reviewers or section tendencies may persist between cycles; previously triaged applications can face a hill to climb if reviewers retain negative impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that some reviewers may carry prior impressions forward; crafting responses to address explicit criticisms and convincing Program Officers about significant changes can help, but new reviewers are not guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI / new investigator status and IC-specific policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Stage Investigator (ESI) status and IC-specific rules (e.g., payline boosts for new investigators) can materially affect outcomes and the advisability of resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult your Program Officer and IC policies—some ICs have favorable treatment for ESIs/new investigators that make resubmission more attractive; POs sometimes provide portfolio-specific insight (e.g., an OP said half of funded ESIs had been triaged initially).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to scrap and start from scratch
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers appeared to 'shrug' at the proposal, or if the revisions required amount to a complete restructure, starting a fresh application may be a better use of effort than incremental resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced PIs often advise scrapping an application that elicited non-constructive comments or where the core idea is judged weak. If major conceptual overhaul is needed, plan a new submission rather than a marginal revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to add new preliminary data or reframe aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Generating new preliminary data, adding a new aim, or extracting a strong aim into a different mechanism can materially change fundability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can realistically produce preliminary data or meaningfully reframe aims before the next submission, do so—examples include converting an R21 into a strengthened R01 or peeling an aim into an R21 that then gains support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional/portfolio considerations and track-record effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Established investigators may enjoy 'triage protection' due to prior track record; institutional funding patterns, payline differences, and portfolio management can affect fairness and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in your career stage, track record, and institutional context. If your track record is strong, you may have more leeway; recognize systemic biases and discuss portfolio-level strategies with Program Officers if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program officer consultation and IC-specific practice (including 'do not resubmit' flags)
rubrics_metrics.description: Program Officers and ICs may have internal practices (including rare 'not suitable for reconsideration' flags) that influence whether resubmission is sensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk to your PO to get IC-specific insight and data; ask whether a 'do not resubmit' category applies or whether PO/IC would support a resubmission. PO input can clarify likely outcomes and strategic options.
